title: At the café
goal: Order food and drinks politely, use *jeg vil gerne have*, and get to know the *tak* culture that governs almost all Danish manners.
bekal: order with *jeg vil gerne have…* and *må jeg få…?*
recognize seven *tak* phrases, each with its own place
wave: Go back over **Unit 5** first: describe your own family out loud, five sentences, without looking at your notes. Watch your choice of *min* and *mit*.

dialogs.title: Dialogue — Frokost på caféen
dialogs.intro: Lunch at a café in Vesterbro. Mette and Budi have just sat down.

lines.speaker: Tjener:
lines.text: Hej! Har I fundet ud af, hvad I vil have?
lines.id: Hi! Have you decided what you'd like?
lines.literal: hi! have you(pl) found out of, what you(pl) will have?

lines.speaker: Mette:
lines.text: Ja. Jeg vil gerne have en kop kaffe og et stykke kage.
lines.id: Yes. I'd like a cup of coffee and a piece of cake.
lines.literal: yes. I will gladly have a cup coffee and a piece cake.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Må jeg få smørrebrød med laks?
lines.id: Could I have the open sandwich with salmon?
lines.literal: may I get butter-bread with salmon?

lines.speaker: Tjener:
lines.text: Selvfølgelig. Vil du have noget at drikke?
lines.id: Of course. Would you like something to drink?
lines.literal: of-course. will you have something to drink?

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.id: Just a glass of water, thanks.

lines.speaker: Tjener:
lines.text: Postevand er gratis. Kommer om lidt!
lines.id: Tap water is free. Coming right up!
lines.literal: pipe-water is free. comes in little!

lines.speaker: Mette:
lines.text: Godt valgt. Smørrebrød er meget dansk.
lines.id: Good choice. Smørrebrød is very Danish.
lines.literal: well chosen. butter-bread is very Danish.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.id: What do people usually drink with it?

lines.speaker: Mette:
lines.text: Øl eller snaps. Men ikke til frokost på en tirsdag.
lines.id: Beer or schnapps. But not for lunch on a Tuesday.
lines.literal: beer or schnapps. but not to lunch on a Tuesday.

notes: **Jeg vil gerne have** is the most important ordering frame in this whole course. Literally "I will gladly have". Without *gerne*, *jeg vil have* sounds like a toddler's demand — rude. That small word changes the whole tone.
**Må jeg få…?** = "may I have…?" A touch more polite again, and the most common way to ask for something another person hands you. *At få* = to get.
**Bare** = "just". A very common softener that makes a request smaller: *bare et glas vand*. Danes use it all the time.
**Postevand** literally means "pipe water" — tap water, which in Denmark is safe to drink and almost always free in cafés. You won't find it in tourist phrasebooks, yet it's useful every day.

**Man** = "one, people, you" in the general sense, like English *one* or generic *you*. *Hvad drikker man?* = "what do people usually drink?" Danish uses it constantly to avoid naming a particular person.
**Om lidt** = "in a moment". Note *om* is used for future time: *om ti minutter* (in ten minutes), *om en uge*, *om et år*. It doesn't mean "about" here.

**Smørrebrød** isn't just a sandwich. It's a single slice of dark rye bread (*rugbrød*) with toppings neatly arranged on top, eaten with a knife and fork, with a serious order of courses: fish first, then meat, then cheese. You'll hear the word everywhere.

grammars.title: Four ways to ask, from most direct to most gentle
body: The choice isn't about right and wrong, but about tone. Notice the steps of the ladder.

head: Form
Example
Tone
rows: Jeg vil gerne have en kaffe.
polite, a bit more of a request
short but fine at a counter

after: Danish **has no word for "please"** like *por favor* or *bitte*. Politeness is carried by *gerne*, by tone of voice, and by *tak* at the end of the sentence. Newcomers looking for a "please" will look forever and never find it.
Instead, *tak* is used far more often than "thank you" in English — including in places where it may feel excessive to you.

grammars.title: Seven tak phrases
body: The word *tak* is the backbone of Danish manners, and it has more jobs than its translation suggests.

head: Phrase
When to use it
rows: all-purpose: thanks, yes please, and sometimes no thanks
accepting an offer — a must; just *ja* feels rude
after a meal, said to whoever cooked — almost compulsory
when you meet again someone who last hosted you

after: ⚠️ *Tak for sidst* ("thanks for last time") has no English equivalent and surprises many newcomers. If someone invites you to dinner and you run into them two weeks later on the street, your first sentence should be *tak for sidst*. Skipping it feels cold.
There's also *tak for i dag* (at the end of a class or meeting), *tak for hjælpen* (thanks for the help) and *tak for i aften*. The pattern: **tak for** + whatever just happened.

blocks.text: ⚠️ *Frokost* means **lunch**, not breakfast — even though it looks like German *Frühstück*, which does mean breakfast. Danish breakfast is *morgenmad* ("morning food"). This mistake makes plenty of people turn up at the wrong time.

*Et stykke* is used to count things that have no unit of their own, like English "a piece of": *et stykke kage* (a piece of cake), *to stykker smørrebrød*. Note the noun has no ending and no plural — it stays bare and singular.

*Jeg spiser ikke svinekød* is worth being able to say without thinking — pork is everywhere in Danish cooking. It's understood without further explanation, and halal food is increasingly easy to find, especially in Nørrebro and around Aarhus.
**Tipping isn't expected in Denmark.** Service is included in the price, and not tipping at all isn't considered rude. If the service was excellent, rounding up is more than enough.

blocks.title: Hygge at the table
items: *Hygge* is often translated "coziness", but it's more precisely a warm atmosphere created deliberately and together. Candles in broad daylight, a table no one hurries away from, relaxed conversation.
The adjective is *hyggelig*: *en hyggelig café*, *et hyggeligt værelse*, *Det var hyggeligt!* — the parting line after a pleasant get-together.
If a Danish host says *Skal vi hygge os?*, they're inviting you to relax together with no agenda. The right answer is always *ja tak*.
I'd like a cup of coffee.
Could I have a glass of water?

exercises.prompt: Soften these rude sentences. Write each one out in full.
Put the words in the right order.
items: gerne / kaffe / vil / jeg / en / have

answers: Jeg vil gerne have en kop kaffe. — Må jeg få et glas vand? — Er der et ledigt bord? — Jeg spiser ikke svinekød. — Må vi bede om regningen? — Det smager rigtig godt.
Ja tak — Nej tak — Tak for mad — Selv tak — Tak for sidst
Jeg vil gerne have en øl. — Må jeg få menuen? — Må jeg bede om regningen? — Jeg vil gerne have et stykke kage. — Må jeg få et glas vand?
